description.text: Learn how net force changes motion, then use F_net = m a to explain and solve problems.

objectives.statement: Choose a system and find its net external force.
State Newton’s second law in words and as F_net = m a.
Calculate force, mass, or acceleration and include direction and units.
Explain balanced forces, mass versus weight, and common errors.

text.text: What you should be able to do

By the end, you should be able to choose the object being analysed, identify every external force, find the net force, predict the direction of acceleration, and calculate its value. You should also be able to explain why a large force does not always produce a large acceleration.
Start with the motion, not the formula

Push an empty trolley and then a loaded trolley with the same effort. The empty trolley changes its motion more easily. Push the same trolley harder and its motion changes more quickly. Newton’s second law gives a precise explanation for both observations.

definition.text: The object or group of objects chosen for analysis. Your force list depends on what you choose as the system.
The vector sum of all external forces acting on the chosen system. Opposing forces must be combined with their directions.
Any change in velocity: speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction.

content.title: Balanced does not mean no forces

text.text: Several forces may act while acceleration is zero. If they balance, the net force is zero. The object can remain at rest or continue at constant velocity.

statement.text: For a constant-mass system in an inertial frame, acceleration is directly proportional to net external force, inversely proportional to mass, and points in the direction of the net force.

conditions.text: This lesson uses classical, constant-mass situations.

caption.text: Net external force equals mass multiplied by acceleration.

conditions.text: Rearrange as a = F_net / m, m = F_net / a, or F_net = m a.

text.text: Mass measures inertia in kilograms. Weight is the gravitational force on a mass and is measured in newtons. Do not substitute weight for mass in F_net = m a.

prompt.text: A 5.0 kg crate is pulled right with 32 N while friction acts left with 12 N. Find its acceleration.

steps.description: Use net force, not the pulling force alone.
Acceleration follows the net force direction.

answer.text: The crate accelerates at 4.0 m/s^2 to the right.

prompt.text: A 2.0 kg cart accelerates at 3.0 m/s^2 east. Find the net force.

steps.description: Force and acceleration have the same direction.

answer.text: The net force is 6.0 N east.

items.text: List the external forces and their directions.
Choose the rearrangement containing the unknown.
Substitute units, state direction, and check whether the result is reasonable.

content.title: Do not choose the largest force

text.text: A 32 N pull and 12 N friction do not produce 32 N of net force. Their resultant is 20 N. Acceleration responds to the vector sum of all external forces.

points.text: Choose a system and find its net external force.
Use F_net = m a with direction and units.
Balanced forces give zero acceleration, not necessarily zero forces.
Mass and weight are different quantities.

prompt.text: Which quantity belongs in F_net = m a?

content.text: The vector sum of all external forces on the chosen system
The object’s weight in every situation
The force pointing in the direction of motion

feedback.text: The law uses the net external force: the vector sum of the external forces on the chosen system.

prompt.text: A book rests on a table. Which statement is correct?

content.text: No forces act on the book.
The upward support and downward weight balance, so net force is zero.
The book has no weight because it is not moving.

feedback.text: Forces act on the book, but they balance. Zero net force means zero acceleration, not zero forces.

hint.text: Ask whether forces balance, not whether forces exist.

prompt.text: A 2.0 kg object has a net force of 10 N east. What is its acceleration?

feedback.text: a = F_net / m = 10 N / 2.0 kg = 5.0 m/s^2 east. Divide by mass and keep the force direction.

prompt.text: The same net force acts on a 2 kg object and a 4 kg object. Which has greater acceleration?

feedback.text: With the same force, a = F_net / m. The smaller mass has the greater acceleration.

prompt.text: A car moves east but slows down. What is true about its acceleration?

content.text: It points east because the car moves east.
It is zero because the car is still moving.
It points west because velocity is changing toward a smaller eastward value.

feedback.text: Acceleration is the change in velocity. Slowing eastward motion requires acceleration westward.

hint.text: Acceleration follows the change in velocity.

claim.text: Mass and weight are the same thing.

correction.text: Mass measures inertia in kilograms; weight is gravitational force in newtons.
Acceleration is determined by the vector sum of all external forces.

claim.text: An object needs a forward force to keep moving forward.

correction.text: A force is needed to change velocity. Constant velocity requires zero net force.

claim.text: Acceleration always points in the direction of motion.

correction.text: Acceleration points in the direction of net force and can oppose motion when an object slows down.

summary.text: Choose a system and find its net external force.
Use F_net = m a with direction and units.
Balanced forces mean zero acceleration, not zero forces.
Use the law to explain calculations and real motion.
